summary: Psalm 135 opens by summoning Yahweh’s servants in his house to praise him. It gives reasons for that praise: Yahweh chose Israel, rules over creation, acted against Egypt and other nations, gave land to Israel, endures through all generations, and is unlike lifeless idols. The psalm closes by calling Israel, Aaron, Levi, and all who fear Yahweh to bless him from Zion.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers many major notes of Book V of Psalms: temple praise, remembered rescue, trust in Yahweh’s rule, and a final call to worship. It places praise on concrete grounds rather than vague feeling.

context.author: No individual author is named. Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections formed over time.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, especially those gathered around Yahweh’s house; later Jewish and Christian communities also received Psalms as prayer and praise.
context.date: Individual psalms may come from different periods from the monarchy through the postexilic period; one date for the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, with this chapter oriented toward Yahweh’s house, Zion, and Jerusalem.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic praise that uses summons, remembered acts, contrast, and repeated commands to praise.

outline.heading: Servants Summoned To Praise
outline.note: The psalm calls those standing in Yahweh’s house to praise Yahweh’s name because he is good and praise is pleasant.

outline.heading: Yahweh’s Choice And Rule
outline.note: The psalm says Yahweh chose Jacob and Israel, is above all gods, does whatever he pleases, and governs heaven, earth, seas, clouds, lightning, rain, and wind.

outline.heading: Remembered Acts For Israel
outline.note: The psalm recalls Yahweh striking Egypt, Pharaoh, nations, and kings, then giving their land as a heritage to Israel.

outline.heading: Enduring Name And Compassion
outline.note: Yahweh’s name and renown endure, and the psalm says he will judge his people and have compassion on his servants.

outline.heading: The Powerlessness Of Idols
outline.note: The idols of the nations are described as human-made silver and gold, unable to speak, see, hear, or breathe; those who make and trust them become like them.

outline.heading: Final Call From Zion
outline.note: Israel, Aaron, Levi, and those who fear Yahweh are called to praise, and the psalm ends blessing Yahweh from Zion and Jerusalem.

keyVerses.text: Praise Yah, for Yahweh is good. Sing praises to his name, for that is pleasant.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the first reason for the chapter’s repeated command to praise: Yahweh’s goodness and the fitting delight of praise.

keyVerses.text: Whatever Yahweh pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth, in the seas and in all deeps.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the psalm’s claim that Yahweh is not limited to one place or power but acts throughout creation.

keyVerses.text: Your name, Yahweh, endures forever; your renown, Yahweh, throughout all generations.
keyVerses.why: This verse turns from remembered acts to Yahweh’s lasting name and reputation.

keyVerses.text: Those who make them will be like them, yes, everyone who trusts in them.
keyVerses.why: This sharpens the idol contrast: the problem is not only that idols are lifeless, but that trust in them reshapes the worshiper.

questions.question: Who is being told to praise Yahweh at the start?
questions.answer: The opening call is directed to “you servants of Yahweh,” especially those who stand in Yahweh’s house and in the courts of God’s house. The setting is worship-oriented, not a private reflection alone.

questions.question: What does “Praise Yah” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “Praise Yah” is a command to praise Yahweh, using the shortened name “Yah.” The psalm begins and ends with this phrase, making praise the frame around everything it remembers.

questions.question: Why does the psalm mention Jacob and Israel?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says Yah chose Jacob and Israel for himself, calling Israel “his own possession.” The psalm treats that choice as one reason the worshiping community should praise Yahweh.

questions.question: Does “above all gods” mean the psalm accepts other gods as equal real powers?
questions.answer: The chapter says Yahweh is “above all gods,” then contrasts him with idols that cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe. It asserts Yahweh’s supremacy rather than equality with other powers: Yahweh acts throughout creation and history, while the images made by human hands are powerless. The poem does not set out a full account of the status of every being called a god.

questions.question: Why does the poem move from weather to Egypt and Canaan?
questions.answer: Verses 6-7 describe Yahweh’s power in creation: heaven, earth, seas, clouds, lightning, rain, and wind. Verses 8-12 then describe Yahweh’s power in Israel’s remembered history, from Egypt to the gift of land as a heritage.

questions.question: Who are Sihon and Og?
questions.answer: In this chapter they are named as defeated kings: Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. The psalm includes them in a short list of nations and kingdoms overcome before Israel received land as a heritage.

questions.question: What does it mean that Yahweh will “judge his people”?
questions.answer: In verse 14, judging his people is paired with having compassion on his servants. The line does not explain the exact legal scene; it presents Yahweh as the one who acts for his people and shows compassion to those who serve him.

questions.question: Why does the psalm mock idols by listing body parts?
questions.answer: The idols have mouths, eyes, ears, and mouths again, but they cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe. The point is that they may resemble living beings, but they lack life and agency.

questions.question: Why are the house of Aaron and house of Levi named separately?
questions.answer: The house of Aaron names the priestly family; the house of Levi names the broader tribe associated with service at the sanctuary. The ancestral worship arrangements distinguish Aaron and his sons’ priesthood from the Levites’ service assisting them. By naming Israel, Aaron, Levi, and all who fear Yahweh, the psalm gathers the wider people and their worshiping groups into one call to praise.

glossary.def: A shortened form of Yahweh’s name used in the repeated call, “Praise Yah.”
Those addressed at the opening and again in verse 14; in this psalm they are connected with standing in Yahweh’s house and receiving Yahweh’s compassion.
A name paired with Israel in verse 4, where the psalm says Yah chose Jacob for himself.
The land given to Israel is called a heritage, meaning something received as a lasting possession.
Objects made of silver and gold by human hands; the psalm says they cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe.
The place named in the final blessing, paired with Jerusalem as the location from which Yahweh is blessed.
